title: Staying Safe · Episode 1
chapters: Get ready: your emergency kit and household plan
Home fires: alarms, escape plans and kitchen fires
Electricity: the danger you can't see

units.t: Staying Safe. Episode one.
In this episode: Get ready: your emergency kit and household plan, Home fires: alarms, escape plans and kitchen fires, Carbon monoxide: the invisible killer and Electricity: the danger you can't see.
Part one. Get ready: your emergency kit and household plan.
When disaster strikes, the decisions you make in the first hour matter most.
A little planning on a quiet weekend can make those decisions almost automatic.
Plan once, calmly.
Imagine your phone buzzes at midnight with an emergency warning and you have half an hour.
Where are the car keys?
What about the dog, the medicines and the passports?
Stress makes clear thinking hard.
The Australian Red Cross and state emergency services urge every household to plan ahead so you do the thinking once, in calm conditions.
Start with your risks.
Northern coasts face cyclones and storm surge, river towns face floods, bushland edges face fire, and cities face heatwaves, storms and outages.
Almost everyone could face a house fire.
Check council and emergency service websites, and ask long-term neighbours who remember past events.
Your household plan.
A plan doesn't need to be complicated.
It should answer a few questions.
When will you leave, and what triggers that decision?
Where will you go: friends or relatives in a safer area, or an evacuation centre?
How will you get there, and what is your backup route if roads close?
How will family members contact each other if phones are down or you're split up?
Many families choose one contact person in another area.
Write key numbers on paper too, in case your phone dies.
The Australian Red Cross offers free planning tools, including its Get Prepared app.
Share the plan with everyone in the household and review it each year.
Kit and pets.
An emergency kit is a collection of supplies stored together.
A common guideline is about three litres of drinking water per person per day for at least three days, plus food needing no cooking or refrigeration.
Add a torch, battery radio, first aid kit, power bank, cash, medicines, glasses and anything needed for babies, older relatives or people with a disability.
Keep document copies in a waterproof bag or saved securely online.
Check the kit every six months.
People have delayed evacuating because of pets.
Microchip them, keep a photo on your phone, pack food, leads and a carrier, and find out which shelters take animals.
Move horses and livestock early.
Staying informed.
Reliable information can decide whether you leave in time.
Australia uses a national warning system with three levels: Advice, Watch and Act, and Emergency Warning.
Each state and territory has its own emergency websites and apps, so find yours before you need them.
The Bureau of Meteorology provides weather and flood warnings, and ABC local radio is an official emergency broadcaster that often keeps going when other services fail.
A battery or wind-up radio helps if power and mobile networks go down.
Be careful with social media: it spreads local news quickly, but rumours and old photos circulate too.
Check official sources before acting, and if your life is in danger, call Triple Zero, 000.
Looking after each other.
In many Australian disasters, the first people to help were neighbours, not police or firefighters.
They checked on older residents, shared generators, moved livestock and offered spare rooms.
Strong local connections are linked to communities coping and recovering better.
Build them simply: swap phone numbers, find out who might need help to evacuate, and join a local community or volunteer group.
If you have a medical condition or disability, tell trusted neighbours what support you may need.
Recovery can take months or years, and stress and grief are normal.
The Australian Red Cross, councils and recovery centres can help.
This is general information, so follow official advice for your area.
The key idea: Planning in calm conditions lets you act quickly in an emergency, so start by learning your local risks.
Part two. Home fires: alarms, escape plans and kitchen fires.
A house fire can make a home deadly in a matter of minutes.
A working smoke alarm and a practised escape plan are the two things most likely to get everyone out alive.
Minutes, not hours.
Real house fires are not like films.
Modern homes are full of synthetic materials such as foam couches, plastics and carpets that burn hot and fast and release thick, toxic smoke.
A room can become deadly within a few minutes.
Smoke, not flames, is usually what kills, filling the air with poisonous gases like carbon monoxide and blocking your sight.
Many fatal fires happen at night.
You can't rely on smelling smoke to wake you.
Australian states and territories require smoke alarms, but rules differ.
In Queensland, from 1 January 2027 every home must have interconnected photoelectric alarms in each bedroom, hallway and level.
Test monthly, clean vents, and replace alarms about ten years old.
Check your state fire service website.
Escape plan and exit.
At 2 am you won't have time to think.
Draw a floor plan and mark two ways out of each room, usually a door and a window.
Make sure security screens and deadlocks open quickly from inside.
Choose a meeting place outside, such as the letterbox.
Practise with everyone, including children, once or twice a year, and teach children to get out, not hide under beds.
In smoke, get low and crawl to the nearest safe exit.
Feel a closed door with the back of your hand; if hot, use another way.
Close doors behind you.
Once out, call 000 and stay out.
Never go back for pets or belongings.
If clothes catch fire: stop, drop, cover your face and roll.
Kitchen fires.
The kitchen is where many house fires start, often when someone leaves food cooking and gets distracted.
Fire services say it neatly: keep looking while cooking.
If a pan of oil or fat catches fire, never throw water on it.
Water sinks under the hot oil, flashes into steam and can blast burning oil across the kitchen.
Instead, if it is safe, turn off the heat and smother the flames by sliding a lid or fire blanket over the pan, then leave it covered until completely cool.
Don't carry the burning pan outside.
A fire blanket near the kitchen exit is cheap and easy to use.
If the fire is spreading or you're unsure, get everyone out, close the door and call Triple Zero, 000.
Heaters, power, batteries.
Winter brings more house fires as heaters, electric blankets and dryers work harder.
Keep heaters at least a metre from curtains, bedding, clothes and furniture, and turn them off when you leave the room or go to bed.
Check electric blankets for frayed cords before winter.
Clean the dryer lint filter every use.
Avoid overloading power boards, and never cover them with rugs.
A newer worry is lithium-ion batteries in e-bikes, e-scooters and power tools.
Damaged or poor-quality batteries can overheat and burn fiercely.
Use the supplied charger, avoid charging bulky batteries overnight or near your exit path, and stop using any battery that is swollen, hot or damaged.
Burns first aid.
If someone is burned, Australian first aid advice is clear: cool the burn under cool running water for 20 minutes.
This helps even if some time has passed.
Remove jewellery and clothing from the area unless stuck to the skin.
Do not use ice, butter, toothpaste or creams.
After cooling, cover the burn loosely with plastic cling wrap or a clean non-stick dressing, and keep the person warm.
Call Triple Zero, 000, for burns that are large, deep, on the face, hands, feet, groin or airway, caused by chemicals or electricity, or on a child or older person.
This is general information only.
A proper first aid course teaches these skills hands-on and is one of the best investments a household can make.
The key idea: Smoke is what kills in house fires, so a working smoke alarm giving early warning is vital.
Part three. Carbon monoxide: the invisible killer.
It has no colour, no smell and no taste, and its symptoms feel like the flu.
Here is how an ordinary heater can quietly poison a home, and how to stop it.
Two brothers.
In May 2010, two brothers, Chase and Tyler Robinson, died in their sleep at their rented home in Mooroopna, near Shepparton in Victoria.
The cause was carbon monoxide from a faulty gas heater.
Nothing had seemed wrong: no smoke, no strange smell, and no alarm, because the home had no carbon monoxide detector.
A coronial inquest examined who was responsible for maintaining the heater.
Their mother, Vanessa Robinson, became a prominent campaigner for gas heater safety, and Victoria has since introduced regular gas safety checks in rental homes.
It is a painful reminder that the most dangerous hazards may be ones we cannot sense.
How it harms.
Carbon monoxide is made when fuels such as gas, wood, charcoal, petrol or diesel burn without enough oxygen.
Red blood cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin.
Carbon monoxide binds to it roughly two hundred times more strongly than oxygen does, so even small amounts steadily push oxygen out of the blood.
The brain and heart suffer first.
The gas is colourless, odourless and tasteless, so people breathe it unaware.
High levels can cause unconsciousness and death within minutes.
Lower levels over hours or days can cause lasting brain and heart damage.
Symptoms that fool.
Early symptoms are ordinary: headache, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, tiredness, weakness, breathlessness and confusion.
People assume flu, migraine or a stomach bug.
Clues point to carbon monoxide instead.
Several people, or pets, feel sick at once.
Symptoms are worse at home or with a heater running, and improve outside.
People who are asleep or have been drinking may lose consciousness before noticing, so night-time poisoning is especially dangerous.
Babies, older people, pregnant women and people with heart or lung disease are more vulnerable.
Sources and servicing.
A major source in Australian homes is gas space heaters, especially older or poorly maintained ones.
An open-flued heater should send fumes out through a flue, but a blocked or faulty flue, or exhaust fans pulling air the wrong way, can spill carbon monoxide inside.
Unflued heaters release fumes into the room and need good ventilation.
Other causes are barbecues, camping stoves, patio heaters or charcoal used indoors, in tents, caravans or garages, generators near open windows, and engines running in closed garages.
Have gas heaters serviced by a licensed gasfitter, generally at least every two years or as the manufacturer recommends.
Warning signs include a yellow or orange flame, soot or stains, and a stuffy room.
If you rent, ask when the heater was last checked.
Alarms and action.
Smoke alarms don't detect carbon monoxide.
A separate alarm from a hardware store warns you when levels rise.
Place it per the instructions, typically near fuel-burning appliances and sleeping areas, and test it regularly.
Requirements for them vary by state and territory, but regulators encourage them, especially with gas heating.
An alarm is a backstop, not a substitute for servicing.
If you suspect poisoning, get everyone, including pets, into fresh air.
If quick and safe, switch off the appliance and open doors on your way out.
Call 000.
Start CPR if someone isn't breathing normally.
Don't return until a licensed gasfitter has checked the source.
Treatment is high-concentration oxygen, and everyone should be assessed.
The key idea: Two young brothers died in 2010 from a faulty gas heater, with no smoke, smell or alarm to warn them.
Part four. Electricity: the danger you can't see.
Electricity gives no warning: no smell, no sound, nothing to see.
A few simple rules, and one small switch in your meter box, stand between ordinary life and a fatal shock.
Why current kills.
Current crossing the chest can throw the heart into a chaotic rhythm called ventricular fibrillation, where it quivers instead of pumping.
That is cardiac arrest.
Current can also make muscles contract so strongly a person can't let go of what they're holding.
And as it passes through tissue, it generates heat and burns along its path.
Entry and exit wounds can look small while muscles, nerves and blood vessels inside are badly damaged.
Anyone who has had a significant shock or electrical burn should be checked by a doctor, even if they feel fine.
Safety switches.
A residual current device, called a safety switch in Australia, constantly compares the current going out along the active wire with the current returning along the neutral.
If they don't match, current is leaking somewhere, possibly through a person.
The switch cuts the power within a fraction of a second, fast enough to greatly reduce the risk of death.
Safety switches differ from circuit breakers and fuses, which mainly protect wiring from overload.
Newer homes must have them, but many older homes have them on only some circuits, or none.
Most have a test button worth pressing regularly.
Leave it to licensed.
Across Australia, it's illegal for an unlicensed person to do electrical wiring work, such as installing power points, replacing light switches or running cables.
Faulty wiring can kill, sometimes years later and for someone else entirely, and a loose connection can start a fire inside a wall.
At home, the habits are simple.
Don't use appliances with frayed or damaged cords.
Don't overload power boards or daisy-chain them.
Keep appliances away from water and never touch switches with wet hands.
Never fish toast from a plugged-in toaster with a knife.
If a switch or power point feels warm or smells of burning, get it checked.
Powerlines down.
After storms, crashes and bushfires, powerlines can lie on the ground, fences, cars or trees.
Treat every fallen line as live, even if it isn't sparking, because it may be re-energised automatically.
Distributors advise staying at least eight metres away, about two car lengths.
Electricity can travel through wet ground, puddles, fences and metal, so you needn't touch the line to be hurt.
Call 000 if someone is injured or there's a fire.
If a line falls on your car, stay inside unless it's on fire.
If you must leave, jump clear with your feet together, never touching the car and ground at the same time, then shuffle away with small steps.
Helping, and looking up.
If someone is being electrocuted, don't grab them.
The current can flow into you too.
Switch off the power at the switchboard or wall, or unplug the appliance if safe.
For powerlines and high voltage, don't approach: call 000 and wait for the electricity company.
Once power is off, check them using DRSABCD, start CPR if needed, send for a defibrillator and cool burns under cool running water for twenty minutes.
Many serious accidents happen outdoors when tall objects meet overhead lines: ladders, tipper trays, boat masts.
Electricity can also arc across a gap.
Look up before raising anything tall, carry long objects horizontally, and never climb poles, towers or train roofs.
The key idea: Electric current can stop the heart and cause deep burns that look small from outside.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why do emergency organisations urge households to plan ahead?
Answer. Stress makes clear thinking hard.
Question two. What usually kills people in house fires?
Answer. Smoke and poisonous gases.
Question three. What made the faulty heater in this case so dangerous?
Answer. The gas gives no smoke, smell or taste to warn you.
Question four. Why should anyone with a significant electric shock see a doctor even if they feel fine?
Answer. Skin wounds can hide serious internal damage.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
